title: A third factor
summary: The spike pair only writes a fading note. A later reward decides whether the note becomes a real change.

terms.definition: A spike pair does not change the weight by itself. A third signal, often a reward, decides whether the eligible pair is applied.
A neuromodulator that can arrive after the spikes. In these models it cashes the eligibility traces that are still alive.
A rule with two spike factors plus a third, slower signal such as reward or dopamine.

cards.text:
Ordinary STDP pays the synapse at the moment of the two spikes.
A reward often arrives later, when those spikes are already over.

The pair writes a fading note, an eligibility trace.
Dopamine, or another third factor, later cashes the notes that are still alive.

lines: Reward at 1 second: the note is still there, and the weight changes.
Reward at 5 seconds: the note is gone. Nothing changes.

question.prompt: A reward that arrives after the eligibility trace has faded still teaches that pair.
question.why: No overlap between the note and the reward means no change.
question.simpler: The third factor has to arrive while the trace is alive.

question.prompt: How many factors does this rule use?
choices: Three: pre, post, and a modulator
question.why: The spikes decide who was eligible. The modulator decides whether to apply it.
question.simpler: Reward alone would change every synapse. The traces pick which ones.

recall.question: What does the third factor do in reward-modulated STDP?
recall.answer: It decides whether a recent spike pair actually changes the weight.

deeper.note: Izhikevich linked STDP to dopamine with an eligibility trace, so a reward that arrives late can still credit the right synapses. The signal can be broadcast. The trace is what makes it specific.

paper.title: Solving the distal reward problem through linkage of STDP and dopamine signaling
